# Vault format golden fixtures

Frozen on-disk artifacts that pin the Encrypted Vaults wire format across both
platforms. **Do not edit or regenerate these to make a test pass.**

## Why these exist

`core:vaultcrypto` (Kotlin) and `ios/.../Sources/VaultCrypto` (Swift) are two
independent implementations of one on-disk format. Every other test on both
sides is a round-trip against itself — encrypt, decrypt, assert you got back
what you put in.

A round-trip cannot catch the failure that actually matters. A
wrong-but-deterministic implementation round-trips perfectly and still cannot
open the other platform's vaults. Worse, the two sides can drift *together*: the
iOS test-support file was written to mirror the shape of Android's tests, so a
shared misunderstanding of the format would have been invisible on both sides
simultaneously.

These fixtures make that detectable, because the format is fully deterministic —
nonces are derived rather than random, and there is no per-file random IV or
salt in the blob. Encrypting fixed inputs must therefore produce **byte-identical**
output on every platform, forever, for a given format version.

## What is pinned

Asserting one file's bytes transitively pins more than it looks like:

| Pinned | How a change shows up |
|---|---|
| HKDF (`Hkdf` / `deriveFileContentKey`) | different content key → every chunk's ciphertext moves |
| AES-GCM usage (key, nonce, AAD wiring) | tag and ciphertext move |
| Per-chunk nonce derivation | chunk ciphertexts move |
| AAD layout (`VaultFormat.chunkAad`) | tags move |
| Header layout and byte order | header assertions fail precisely |
| Chunk-count rule and final-chunk flag | final chunk's tag moves |

Notably HKDF has no known-answer test of its own on either platform. Until one
lands (`docs/TEST_COVERAGE_PRD.md` Phase 3), this fixture is what stops it
drifting.

## `v1/golden.vault`

Format version 1. 228 bytes = 30-byte header + 150 bytes plaintext + 3 × 16-byte
GCM tags.

Generated by the **Android** writer — one generator, one source of truth. iOS
only ever verifies.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| VMK | 32 bytes, `vmk[i] = i` (0x00…0x1F) |
| file id | 16 bytes, `fileId[i] = 0xA0 + i` |
| chunk size | 64 bytes |
| plaintext | 150 bytes, `plaintext[i] = (i * 7 + 11) % 251` |

Chunk size is deliberately tiny so 150 bytes spans three chunks (64 + 64 + 22),
exercising multi-chunk nonce derivation and a partial final chunk. The plaintext
is defined by formula rather than shipped as a second file so both languages
reproduce it exactly with no text-encoding questions.

These values are not secrets and are never used outside tests. Being public and
boring is the point.

`sha256(v1/golden.vault) = 2959e91095452f54a38f1e1440395363c4e6f1e0547edc25311cccb6f864c768`

## Tests that consume this

- `core/vaultcrypto/src/test/kotlin/.../GoldenVaultInteropTest.kt`
- `ios/LibraVaultApp/LibraVault/LibraVaultTests/GoldenVaultInteropTests.swift`

Both assert the writer reproduces the file byte-for-byte *and* that the reader
recovers the exact plaintext from it. Keep the two in sync.

## If a test against this fixture fails

You changed the wire format. That is not automatically wrong, but it is never
incidental:

- **Deliberate change** — bump `VaultFormat.FORMAT_VERSION`, add a *new*
  `v<N>/golden.vault` beside this one, and keep the v1 fixture and its tests, so
  vaults already on users' devices stay readable.
- **Unintended change** — you have just broken every existing vault. Fix the
  code, not the fixture.

Regenerating (deliberately, and it lands in review as a changed binary):

```bash
VAULTCRYPTO_REGENERATE_GOLDEN=true \
  ./gradlew :core:vaultcrypto:testDebugUnitTest --tests '*GoldenVaultInteropTest*'
```
